newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti's PCs face end of line.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti's PCs face end of line.

text.p: Olivetti's problem personal computer company, the source of much anguish and heavy losses for the Italian information technology group in the 1990s, looks like it faces the end of the line.

Olivetti is talking about streamlining the loss-making PC business, but analysts on Thursday saw few groups willing to buy or form an alliance with the unit. Closure is seen by some as the most likely outcome.

The PC company -- Olivetti Personal Computers -- has consistently lost money in the 1990s and is becoming such a small player in the global market that it appears unlikely to tempt one of Europe's few remaining computer players or any major U.S. firms.

"It is unrealistic to think that Olivetti can sell their PC business, if they could it would have been done already. The only real option is to close it down," said one London-based industry analyst with an Italian bank.

At risk could be about 1,800 jobs, largely at Olivetti's Scarmagno plant near the group's Ivrea headquarters in north-west Italy, and the survival of one of Europe's last players in the fiercely competitive field.
"Olivetti simply can't get their costs down quickly enough, and the number of PCs they need to sell to break even is always just tantalisingly out of reach," one industry analyst said.

Former group chairman Carlo De Benedetti said if the PC company did not break even this year it would be sold off. But he resigned late on Tuesday after a boardroom battle with recently-appointed chief executive Francesco Caio.

Caio said on Wednesday the PC firm would not break even in 1996 but did not repeat De Benedetti's ultimatum -- possibly for fear of angering Italy's unions and to keep alive any lingering hopes of finding a partner.

After speaking to the company late on Wednesday, analysts said they believed Caio's aim was to address the company's problem of not selling enough PCs to large corporate customers and then look for a sale or to form an alliance.
Analysts said the problem was that Olivetti had probably been looking to sell off its PC unit for at least 12 months but had found no buyers looking for spare PC capacity in Europe.

The Olivetti PC company lost 200 billion lire ($132.5 million) in 1995. Caio said it lost 10 billion lire at the operating level in the first half of 1996, while the entire Olivetti group lost a shock 440.2 billion lire before tax.

Olivetti's group loss included a 200 billion lire provision as the company accelerates "the reduction of its presence in the hardware sector". Most analysts assume this means the PC unit but the charge would not cover shutting the business down.
They say it would take a minimum of 400 billion lire to lay off staff and exit from any leases it holds.
There would be further costs of writing off inventories and getting out of contracts with other producers. For example all Olivetti laptop computers are made by a company in Taiwan.
The only company thought to have talked seriously to Olivetti is French computer group Bull, which has now allied itself to Bell Packard of the U.S.
Europe's computer industry is on the back foot in its own backyard. Vobis, Escom, ICL, Bull and Olivetti are all in retreat or have already surrendered.

The biggest winners have been the Americans with IBM, Dell and Hewlett-Packard all winning ground in Europe, but these, together with the world's top PC maker Compaq, in the words of one analyst "need extra capacity like a hole in the head." ($1=1509 Lire)
